meaning.text: Afanasyev explains that the names вѣдунъ and вѣдьма (also вѣдунья, вѣщица) come from the root вѣд-, вѣщ- and denote knowing people endowed with a spirit of foreknowledge and prophecy, a poetic gift and the art of healing illnesses.
Afanasyev treats the Serbian вѣштица as the same figure as the вѣдьма, writing "the soul of the вѣдьма (вѣштица)".

appearance.text: Outwardly witches look no different from ordinary mortals.
Apart from that, a witch has a small tail which she carefully hides.
At night witches let their braids down loose over their shoulders.
At night, having stripped naked, witches put on long white ungirdled shifts (or shrouds).

scene.text: The Serbian vještica flies about at night, shining like fire as she flies.
Vještice gather mostly on the threshing floor.
Villagers tell that when a witch gathers dew, milks other people's cows or makes twisted knots (заломы) in the fields, she is always in a white shift with her hair loose.
At night witches fly out through chimneys to do harm or to revel on the Bald Mountain (лысая гора).

appearance.text: According to folk tales, the devilish spirit inside a vještica leaves her in sleep and turns into a butterfly.
The spirit may instead turn into a hen.
The spirit may instead turn into a turkey.
Serbs say the soul of the witch flies out of her in sleep in the form of a butterfly or a bird.
While the spirit is out of her, the woman lies as if dead.

behavior_habitat.text: In that shape the spirit flies about houses and eats people, especially small children.
Finding a person asleep, she strikes him with a rod over the left breast, the chest opens, and she takes out the heart and eats it, after which the chest grows together again.
Some people eaten this way die at once; others live on as long as she decreed when she ate the heart, and die the death she assigned them.
Vještice are said to eat people most of all at the Shrovetides (покладе).
When she wants to fly from the house, she smears some ointment under her armpits and says "ni o trn ni o grm, već na pometno gumno" (not against thorn nor bush, but onto the swept threshing floor).
A tale tells of a woman who was not a vještica, used the ointment, said by mistake "against thorn and against bush", and was battered all over as she flew.
If someone turns the sleeping woman's head to where her feet were while the spirit is out, she will never wake again.
Afanasyev reports the same Serbian belief: if the witch is turned head to foot while her soul wanders, the returning soul cannot find its way in and she never wakes.
By Russian belief, witches ride to the Bald Mountain for the Kupala gathering not only on brooms but also on swift, tireless steeds.
In tales they give heroes wonderful flying horses.
In the Ukraine people are still convinced that there is no village without a witch.
In Little Russia it is told that witches steal rain and dew from the sky, carrying them off in tied-up jugs or sacks and hiding them in their huts and storerooms.
The common folk look for witches among themselves and will point out particular people of their own village as a witch and advise caution.
People turn to them in need for help and advice, and blame them for all public and private misfortunes.
Wishing to cause drought, a witch waves her apron at a rain cloud as soon as it appears, and the cloud leaves the horizon.
The "Slovenian" (словенскія) вѣштицы, like the vilas, possess deadly arrows.
At night witches sit on brooms, brew a magic potion in pots, and fly off with the rising steam through the chimneys.

dealing_with_it.text: Vještice do not eat garlic, so many people smear garlic on their chests, the soles of their feet and under their armpits at the white and Christmas Shrovetides.
Once a vještica confesses and owns up, she can no longer eat people, but becomes a healer and gives herbs to those she has eaten.

When many children or people die in a village and all accuse some woman of being a vještica who ate them, they bind her and throw her into water to see whether she can sink, because they say a vještica cannot sink.
Serbs take a butterfly flying in the evening for the soul of a vještica, try to catch it and singe its wings.

origin.text: A vještica is a woman who, according to folk tales, has some devilish spirit inside her.
No young and beautiful woman is called a vještica, only old women.

rationale.text: Karadžić records the vještica as a Serbian belief in his 1818 and 1852 dictionaries, which count as one source.
Afanasyev's Serbian passage on the вѣштица cites Karadžić's Srpski rječnik and quotes its entry, so for Serbs it is not independent of Karadžić.
Afanasyev equates the вѣдьма with the Serbian вѣштица ("душа вѣдьмы (вѣштицы)").
Afanasyev records the вѣдьма for Russians and in the Ukraine and Little Russia from collections other than Karadžić.

Three peoples therefore rest on two independent 19th-century collectors: Karadžić for Serbs, Afanasyev for Russians and Ukrainians; no single people has two independent sources, and the link between them is Afanasyev's equation.
